prompt:
*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

A division is *proportional* if each of the $n$ players receives total value at least $\frac1n$ by their own value function.

Goods $A,B,C$ are indivisible and are divided between two players. For each of the following value tables, find a proportional division, or write "no proportional division".

(i) $$\begin{array}{c|cc} & v_1 & v_2 \\ \hline A & 0.4 & 1.0 \\ B & 0.3 & 0 \\ C & 0.3 & 0\end{array}$$
(ii) $$\begin{array}{c|cc} & v_1 & v_2 \\ \hline A & 0.6 & 0.6 \\ B & 0.4 & 0 \\ C & 0 & 0.4\end{array}$$
(iii) $$\begin{array}{c|cc} & v_1 & v_2 \\ \hline A & 0.3 & 0.3 \\ B & 0.5 & 0.5 \\ C & 0.2 & 0.2\end{array}$$
answer: (i) Player 1: $\{B,C\}$, Player 2: $\{A\}$. (ii) No proportional division. (iii) Player 1: $\{A,C\}$, Player 2: $\{B\}$.

solutions.title: Check each table
solutions.body:
Proportional means each player gets at least $\frac12$.

(i) Player 2 values only $A$, so Player 2 must get $A$. Then Player 1 gets $\{B,C\}$, worth $0.3+0.3=0.6\ge\frac12$. Division: 1: $\{B,C\}$, 2: $\{A\}$.

(ii) Player 1 needs $A$ (without $A$ they have at most $0.4$), and Player 2 needs $A$ too (without $A$, at most $0.4$). Both cannot receive $A$, so there is no proportional division.

(iii) The values are identical for both players: $A=0.3$, $B=0.5$, $C=0.2$. Give $B$ to one player ($0.5$) and $\{A,C\}$ to the other ($0.3+0.2=0.5$): 1: $\{A,C\}$, 2: $\{B\}$.

*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

A division is *proportional* if each of the $n$ players receives total value at least $\frac1n$ by their own value function.

Suppose every good in $G$ is divisible and homogeneous. Prove that a proportional division always exists.
answer: Give each player $\frac1n$ of every good.

solutions.title: Equal shares
solutions.body: Give each of the $n$ players the fraction $\frac1n$ of every good. By linearity, player $i$ receives total value $\frac1n\sum_{g\in G}v_i(g)=\frac1n v_i(G)=\frac1n$. So every player receives exactly $\frac1n$, and the division is proportional. ∎

prompt:
*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

A division is *proportional* if each of the $n$ players receives total value at least $\frac1n$ by their own value function. It is *super proportional* if each player receives total value strictly greater than $\frac1n$.

Suppose every good in $G$ is divisible and homogeneous. Prove that a super proportional division exists if and only if not all players have the same value function.
answer: A super proportional division exists iff the players' value functions are not all identical (start from equal shares and let each player make a small mutually beneficial trade with a player whose values differ).

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**($\Rightarrow$)** Suppose all players have the same value function $v$ and let player $i$ receive fraction $x_{ig}$ of good $g$ (so $\sum_ix_{ig}=1$). The total value received by all players is $\sum_i\sum_g x_{ig}v(g)=\sum_gv(g)=1$. If every player received more than $\frac1n$, the sum would exceed $1$, a contradiction. So no super proportional division exists.

**($\Leftarrow$)** Suppose not all value functions coincide ($n\ge2$). Start from the equal split in which each player has $\frac1n$ of every good, worth exactly $\frac1n$ to everyone.

*Claim.* If $v_i\ne v_j$, there are goods $g,h$ with $v_i(g)v_j(h)>v_j(g)v_i(h)$. Indeed, if all the cross products $v_i(g)v_j(h)-v_j(g)v_i(h)$ vanished then the vectors $(v_i(g))_g$ and $(v_j(g))_g$ would be proportional; since both sum to $1$ they would be equal. So some cross product is nonzero; swap names of $g,h$ if necessary to make it positive.

With such $g,h$ we have $v_i(g)>0$ and $v_j(h)>0$ and $\frac{v_i(h)}{v_i(g)}<\frac{v_j(h)}{v_j(g)}$ (the right side is $+\infty$ if $v_j(g)=0$). Pick $r$ strictly between. Let player $i$ give an amount $\varepsilon$ of $h$ to $j$ and receive an amount $\delta=r\varepsilon$ of $g$ from $j$. Then $i$ gains $\delta v_i(g)-\varepsilon v_i(h)=\varepsilon\big(rv_i(g)-v_i(h)\big)>0$ and $j$ gains $\varepsilon v_j(h)-\delta v_j(g)=\varepsilon\big(v_j(h)-rv_j(g)\big)>0$. Both strictly gain.

Now, since not all functions agree, every player $i$ has a partner $p(i)$ with $v_{p(i)}\ne v_i$ (otherwise everyone would equal $v_i$). For each $i$ perform such a trade $T_i$ between $i$ and $p(i)$, with all amounts $\varepsilon$ so tiny that the total amount taken from any player's holding of any good is less than $\frac1n$ (at most $2n$ trades touch a given player). Values are additive, so each player's total value is $\frac1n$ plus the sum of the gains from the trades they take part in; each such gain is strictly positive and every player takes part in at least one trade ($T_i$). Hence everybody gets strictly more than $\frac1n$. ∎

prompt:
*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

A division is *envy-free* if for all players $i\ne j$, $v_i(G_i)\ge v_i(G_j)$, where $G_k$ is what player $k$ receives.

Goods $A,B,C,D$ are indivisible and are divided among three players. For each table find an envy-free division, or write "no envy-free division".

(i) $$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \\ \hline A & 0.25 & 0.3 & 0.5 \\ B & 0.25 & 0.4 & 0 \\ C & 0.25 & 0.2 & 0 \\ D & 0.25 & 0.1 & 0.5\end{array}$$
(ii) $$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \\ \hline A & 0.25 & 0.3 & 0.1 \\ B & 0.25 & 0.3 & 0.2 \\ C & 0.25 & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ D & 0.25 & 0.2 & 0.4\end{array}$$
answer: (i) Player 1: $\{C,D\}$, Player 2: $\{B\}$, Player 3: $\{A\}$. (ii) No envy-free division.

solutions.title: Part (i)
solutions.body:
Give Player 1 $\{C,D\}$, Player 2 $\{B\}$, Player 3 $\{A\}$.
- Player 1 receives $0.5$; sees $\{B\}$ and $\{A\}$ as $0.25$ each.
- Player 2 receives $0.4$; sees $\{A\}=0.3$ and $\{C,D\}=0.3$.
- Player 3 receives $0.5$ (good $A$); sees $\{B\}=0$ and $\{C,D\}=0.5$.

Nobody prefers another bundle, so the division is envy-free.

solutions.title: Part (ii)
solutions.body: Everybody values every good positively, so anyone who gets nothing envies someone; hence the bundles have sizes $2,1,1$ in some order. Player 1 values every good at $0.25$, so a player holding one good envies a player holding two; thus Player 1 must be the one with two goods (if Player 1 held one good, the other two players could hold at most one each, only $3$ goods in total). Now Player 2 holds a single good, worth at most $0.3$, while Player 1's pair is worth at least $0.2+0.2=0.4$ to Player 2. So Player 2 is envious. Hence no envy-free division exists.

prompt:
*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

A division is *proportional* if each of the $n$ players receives total value at least $\frac1n$ by their own value function. A division is *envy-free* if for all players $i\ne j$, $v_i(G_i)\ge v_i(G_j)$, where $G_k$ is what player $k$ receives.

Prove that every envy-free division is also proportional.
answer: If someone gets less than $\frac1n$, they value the other $n-1$ bundles at more than $1-\frac1n$ in total, so some bundle is worth more than $\frac1n$ to them.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body: Suppose an envy-free division gives player $i$ total value $v_i(G_i)<\frac1n$. The other $n-1$ bundles together are worth $1-v_i(G_i)>\frac{n-1}n$ to player $i$ (the bundles partition $G$), so one of them, $G_j$, has $v_i(G_j)>\frac{1}{n-1}\cdot\frac{n-1}n=\frac1n>v_i(G_i)$. Then player $i$ envies $j$, contradiction. So everyone receives at least $\frac1n$. ∎

answer: Yes: in a proportional division each player has at least $\frac12$, so the other bundle is worth at most $\frac12$ to them.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body: Let the division be proportional with two players. Player $i$ receives $v_i(G_i)\ge\frac12$, and the other bundle is the rest of $G$, so $v_i(G_j)=1-v_i(G_i)\le\frac12\le v_i(G_i)$. Hence no one envies the other. ∎

With three players, is every proportional division also envy-free? Prove, or disprove by finding a counterexample.
answer: No. With the table below, giving $A,B,C$ to Players 1, 2, 3 is proportional but not envy-free.

solutions.title: Counterexample
solutions.body:
Three players, indivisible goods $A,B,C$ with
$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \\ \hline A & 0.4 & 0.6 & 0 \\ B & 0 & 0.4 & 0.6 \\ C & 0.6 & 0 & 0.4\end{array}$$
Give $A$ to Player 1, $B$ to Player 2, $C$ to Player 3. Player 1 gets $0.4$, Player 2 gets $0.4$, Player 3 gets $0.4$: all more than $\frac13$, so the division is proportional. But Player 1 values Player 3's good $C$ at $0.6>0.4$, so Player 1 envies Player 3. Hence proportional does not imply envy-free for three players.

prompt:
*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

A division $d_1$ *dominates* $d_2$ if at least one player gets strictly greater total value in $d_1$ and no player gets less. A division is *Pareto efficient* if no division dominates it.

Goods $A,B,C,D$ are indivisible and divided between two players with
$$\begin{array}{c|cc} & v_1 & v_2 \\ \hline A & 0.3 & 0.1 \\ B & 0.3 & 0.2 \\ C & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ D & 0.2 & 0.4\end{array}$$List all Pareto efficient divisions and say whether each is proportional.
answer: There are five Pareto efficient divisions: (1: all; 2: none), (1: $\{A,B,C\}$; 2: $\{D\}$), (1: $\{A,B\}$; 2: $\{C,D\}$), (1: $\{A\}$; 2: $\{B,C,D\}$), (1: none; 2: all). Only the third, 1: $\{A,B\}$, 2: $\{C,D\}$, is proportional.

solutions.title: Enumerate the 16 divisions
solutions.body:
For each set $S$ given to Player 1 (the rest to Player 2), the pair (value to 1, value to 2) is:

$\varnothing$: $(0,1)$; $A$: $(0.3,0.9)$; $B$: $(0.3,0.8)$; $C$: $(0.2,0.7)$; $D$: $(0.2,0.6)$; $AB$: $(0.6,0.7)$; $AC$: $(0.5,0.6)$; $AD$: $(0.5,0.5)$; $BC$: $(0.5,0.5)$; $BD$: $(0.5,0.4)$; $CD$: $(0.4,0.3)$; $ABC$: $(0.8,0.4)$; $ABD$: $(0.8,0.3)$; $ACD$: $(0.7,0.2)$; $BCD$: $(0.7,0.1)$; $ABCD$: $(1,0)$.

The non-dominated pairs are $(0,1)$, $(0.3,0.9)$, $(0.6,0.7)$, $(0.8,0.4)$, $(1,0)$; every other pair is dominated by one of these (for instance $(0.3,0.8)\le(0.3,0.9)$, $(0.5,0.6)\le(0.6,0.7)$, $(0.8,0.3)\le(0.8,0.4)$, $(0.7,0.2)\le(0.8,0.4)$).

So the Pareto efficient divisions are: 1 gets everything; 1 gets $\{A,B,C\}$ and 2 gets $\{D\}$; 1 gets $\{A,B\}$ and 2 gets $\{C,D\}$; 1 gets $\{A\}$ and 2 gets $\{B,C,D\}$; 2 gets everything.

Proportional means both values are at least $0.5$: only $(0.6,0.7)$, i.e. 1: $\{A,B\}$, 2: $\{C,D\}$.

prompt:
*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

A division is *proportional* if each of the $n$ players receives total value at least $\frac1n$ by their own value function. A division $d_1$ *dominates* $d_2$ if at least one player gets strictly greater total value in $d_1$ and no player gets less. A division is *Pareto efficient* if no division dominates it.

Goods $A,B,C$ are indivisible and are divided between two players. Choose value functions for the two players and find a proportional division that is not Pareto efficient.
answer: For example $v_1=(0.5,0,0.5)$, $v_2=(0,0.5,0.5)$ on $(A,B,C)$: the division 1: $\{A,B\}$, 2: $\{C\}$ is proportional but dominated.

solutions.title: Example
solutions.body:
Take
$$\begin{array}{c|cc} & v_1 & v_2 \\ \hline A & 0.5 & 0 \\ B & 0 & 0.5 \\ C & 0.5 & 0.5\end{array}$$
The division 1: $\{A,B\}$, 2: $\{C\}$ gives Player 1 value $0.5$ and Player 2 value $0.5$, so it is proportional. But 1: $\{A,C\}$, 2: $\{B\}$ gives Player 1 value $1$ and Player 2 value $0.5$: nobody is worse off and Player 1 is strictly better off, so the first division is not Pareto efficient.

prompt:
*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

A division $d_1$ *dominates* $d_2$ if at least one player gets strictly greater total value in $d_1$ and no player gets less. A division is *Pareto efficient* if no division dominates it.

Let $G$ be a set of divisible, homogeneous goods. Prove, or disprove by finding a counterexample: a division is not Pareto efficient if and only if there are goods $g$ and $g'$ in $G$ such that a trade between two players of a part of $g$ for a part of $g'$ yields a division that dominates the given one.
answer: False (the "only if" direction fails). With three players and the table below, the division 1: $A$, 2: $B$, 3: $C$ is not Pareto efficient, yet no pairwise trade dominates it.

solutions.title: Counterexample
solutions.body:
The "if" direction is true (a dominating trade shows the division is not Pareto efficient), but the "only if" direction fails with three players. Take
$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \\ \hline A & 0.4 & 0.6 & 0 \\ B & 0 & 0.4 & 0.6 \\ C & 0.6 & 0 & 0.4\end{array}$$
and the division 1: $A$, 2: $B$, 3: $C$ (each gets $0.4$). The cyclic division 1: $C$, 2: $A$, 3: $B$ gives each player $0.6$, so it dominates; hence the division is not Pareto efficient.

But no trade between two players helps: Player 1 holds $A$ and Player 2 holds $B$, and Player 1 values $B$ at $0$, so any trade of part of $A$ for part of $B$ makes Player 1 strictly worse off; Player 2 holds $B$ and Player 3 holds $C$, and Player 2 values $C$ at $0$ (strictly worse off); Player 3 holds $C$ and Player 1 holds $A$, and Player 3 values $A$ at $0$ (strictly worse off). So no trade between two players yields a dominating division, and the statement is false.

prompt:
*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

Suppose Player 1 values good $g_i$ at least as much as Player 2 does, and Player 2 values $g_j$ at least as much as Player 1 does: $v_1(g_i)\ge v_2(g_i)$ and $v_2(g_j)\ge v_1(g_j)$. In some division Player 1 possesses a fraction $s$ ($0<s\le1$) of $g_i$, and Player 2 possesses a fraction $t$ ($0<t\le1$) of $g_j$. Prove that if a trade of Player 1's fraction $s$ of $g_i$ for Player 2's fraction $t$ of $g_j$ increases either player's total value, then the other player's total value must decrease.
answer: If Player 1 gains then $t\,v_2(g_j)\ge t\,v_1(g_j)>s\,v_1(g_i)\ge s\,v_2(g_i)$, so Player 2 loses; symmetrically if Player 2 gains.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
After the trade Player 1's value changes by $t\,v_1(g_j)-s\,v_1(g_i)$ and Player 2's by $s\,v_2(g_i)-t\,v_2(g_j)$.

If Player 1 gains, $t\,v_1(g_j)>s\,v_1(g_i)$, hence $t\,v_2(g_j)\ge t\,v_1(g_j)>s\,v_1(g_i)\ge s\,v_2(g_i)$, so Player 2's change is negative.

If Player 2 gains, $s\,v_2(g_i)>t\,v_2(g_j)$, hence $s\,v_1(g_i)\ge s\,v_2(g_i)>t\,v_2(g_j)\ge t\,v_1(g_j)$, so Player 1's change is negative. ∎

prompt:

Suppose Player 1 possesses a fraction $s$ ($0<s\le1$) of $g_i$, and Player 2 possesses a fraction $t$ ($0<t\le1$) of $g_j$, in some division, and (all values being positive)
$$\frac{v_1(g_j)}{v_2(g_j)}\le\frac{v_1(g_i)}{v_2(g_i)}.$$
Prove that if a trade of Player 1's fraction of $g_i$ for Player 2's fraction of $g_j$ increases either player's total value, then the other player's total value must decrease.
answer: The ratio condition gives $\frac{v_1(g_j)}{v_1(g_i)}\le\frac{v_2(g_j)}{v_2(g_i)}$; if Player 1 gains then $\frac st<\frac{v_1(g_j)}{v_1(g_i)}\le\frac{v_2(g_j)}{v_2(g_i)}$, so Player 2 loses; symmetrically.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
Rearranging the hypothesis gives $\dfrac{v_1(g_j)}{v_1(g_i)}\le\dfrac{v_2(g_j)}{v_2(g_i)}$.

If Player 1 gains, $t\,v_1(g_j)>s\,v_1(g_i)$, so $\dfrac st<\dfrac{v_1(g_j)}{v_1(g_i)}\le\dfrac{v_2(g_j)}{v_2(g_i)}$, i.e. $s\,v_2(g_i)<t\,v_2(g_j)$: Player 2 loses.

If Player 2 gains, $s\,v_2(g_i)>t\,v_2(g_j)$, so $\dfrac st>\dfrac{v_2(g_j)}{v_2(g_i)}\ge\dfrac{v_1(g_j)}{v_1(g_i)}$, i.e. $s\,v_1(g_i)>t\,v_1(g_j)$: Player 1 loses. ∎

prompt:
*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

The *Adjusted Winner Procedure* for two players and divisible homogeneous goods $g_1,\dots,g_k$ (all values positive): let $G_1=\{g:v_1(g)>v_2(g)\}$, $G_2=\{g:v_2(g)>v_1(g)\}$, $G_r$ the ties, and assume $v_1(G_1)\ge v_2(G_2)$. Tentatively give $G_1\cup G_r$ to Player 1 and $G_2$ to Player 2. Order the goods so that $\frac{v_1(g_{i_1})}{v_2(g_{i_1})}\ge\dots\ge\frac{v_1(g_{i_k})}{v_2(g_{i_k})}$; Player 1 then holds $g_{i_1},\dots,g_{i_r}$ (all goods with ratio $\ge1$). If the total values are not equal, Player 1 gives goods or fractions of goods to Player 2 in the order $g_{i_r},g_{i_{r-1}},\dots$ until both players have the same total value.

A division $d_1$ *dominates* $d_2$ if at least one player gets strictly greater total value in $d_1$ and no player gets less. A division is *Pareto efficient* if no division dominates it. A division is *envy-free* if for all players $i\ne j$, $v_i(G_i)\ge v_i(G_j)$, where $G_k$ is what player $k$ receives.

Using earlier parts, prove that the procedure terminates and yields a division that is both envy-free and Pareto efficient.
answer: Termination follows from the intermediate value theorem; the final division maximizes $v_1+\theta v_2$ for some $\theta>0$, hence is Pareto efficient; equal values $x<\frac12$ would be dominated by swapping the bundles, so $x\ge\frac12$ and the division is envy-free.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
*Termination.* At the start Player 1 has value $W_1\ge W_2$, Player 2's value. As Player 1 hands over $g_{i_r}$, then $g_{i_{r-1}}$, ..., continuously, Player 1's value decreases continuously and Player 2's increases continuously. If everything were handed over, Player 1 would have value $0$ and Player 2 value $1$. So the difference (Player 1's value minus Player 2's) is continuous, is $\ge0$ at the start and is $-1<0$ at the end. By the intermediate value theorem it is $0$ at some point (reached after finitely many goods are touched), and the procedure stops there with both players having the same value $x$.

*Pareto efficiency.* Because of the order of transfers, the final division has the following shape: for some ratio $\theta\ge1$, Player 1 holds all of every good with ratio $\frac{v_1}{v_2}>\theta$, Player 2 holds all of every good with ratio $<\theta$, and goods with ratio exactly $\theta$ may be split. (If the process stops exactly at the boundary where all remaining goods of Player 1 have $v_2=0$, any $\theta\ge1$ at least as large as the largest finite ratio works.) Let $p_g$ be the fraction of $g$ held by Player 1. For any division with fractions $p'_g$,
$$v_1+\theta v_2=\sum_g\Big(p'_g\,v_1(g)+\theta(1-p'_g)v_2(g)\Big)=\theta+\sum_gp'_g\big(v_1(g)-\theta v_2(g)\big),$$
which is largest when $p'_g=1$ if $v_1(g)>\theta v_2(g)$ and $p'_g=0$ if $v_1(g)<\theta v_2(g)$. The final division has exactly this form, so it maximizes $v_1+\theta v_2$ over all divisions. If some division dominated it, then $v_1'\ge x$, $v_2'\ge x$ with one inequality strict, so $v'_1+\theta v_2'>x+\theta x$, contradicting maximality (as $\theta>0$). So it is Pareto efficient. (Equivalently, any further trade that helps one player must hurt the other, by 4(a) and 4(b).)

*Envy-freeness.* Both players end with value $x$, so each values the other's bundle at $1-x$. If $x<\frac12$, swapping the two bundles would give each player $1-x>x$, a division dominating the final one, contradicting Pareto efficiency. Hence $x\ge\frac12\ge1-x$ and neither player envies the other. ∎

prompt:
*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

*Divide and Choose* (two players): one player (the divider) splits $G$ into two sets, each worth exactly $\frac12$ to the divider; the other player chooses the set she prefers (by her own values) and the divider gets the remaining set.

Let $G$ be a cake with three divisible, homogeneous regions $C$ (chocolate), $V$ (vanilla) and $S$ (strawberry), and
$$\begin{array}{c|cc} & v_1 & v_2 \\ \hline C & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ V & 0.3 & 0.4 \\ S & 0.5 & 0.3\end{array}$$If both players follow the procedure exactly (either player may be the divider), which of the following divisions could result? For each, say whether it is possible and, if so, which player was the divider.

(i) $\{1:(S),\ 2:(C,V)\}$
(ii) $\{1:(C,V),\ 2:(S)\}$
(iii) $\{1:(V,\tfrac12S),\ 2:(C,\tfrac12S)\}$
(iv) $\{1:(\tfrac12V,S),\ 2:(C,\tfrac12V)\}$
answer: (i) possible, Player 1 divided; (ii) not possible; (iii) not possible; (iv) possible, Player 2 divided.

solutions.title: Check each
solutions.body:
The divider's two bundles must each be worth exactly $\frac12$ to the divider, and the chooser must take a bundle that is at least as good for her.

(i) Player 1 as divider: $S$ is worth $0.5$ and $\{C,V\}$ is worth $0.2+0.3=0.5$ to Player 1. Player 2 values $\{C,V\}$ at $0.7>0.3$, so she picks $\{C,V\}$ and Player 1 keeps $S$. **Possible; Player 1 was the divider.**

(ii) If Player 1 divided into $\{C,V\}$ and $\{S\}$, Player 2 would choose $\{C,V\}$ (worth $0.7$), leaving Player 1 with $S$, not this outcome. If Player 2 divided, the bundles must be worth $\frac12$ to her, but $\{C,V\}=0.7$ and $\{S\}=0.3$. **Not possible.**

(iii) Player 1 would get $0.3+0.25=0.55\ne\frac12$ and Player 2 would get $0.3+0.15=0.45\ne\frac12$. Whoever the divider is, their own bundle must be worth exactly $\frac12$ to them. **Not possible.**

(iv) Player 2's bundle $\{C,\frac12V\}$ is worth $0.3+0.2=0.5$ to her and so is $\{\frac12V,S\}$ ($0.2+0.3$), so Player 2 can be the divider. Player 1 values $\{\frac12V,S\}$ at $0.15+0.5=0.65>0.35$, so Player 1 chooses it. **Possible; Player 2 was the divider.**

prompt:
*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

A division is *envy-free* if for all players $i\ne j$, $v_i(G_i)\ge v_i(G_j)$, where $G_k$ is what player $k$ receives. *Divide and Choose* (two players): one player (the divider) splits $G$ into two sets, each worth exactly $\frac12$ to the divider; the other player chooses the set she prefers (by her own values) and the divider gets the remaining set.

Prove, or disprove by finding a counterexample, that Divide and Choose always results in an envy-free division.
answer: True. The divider values both sets equally; the chooser takes the set she prefers.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body: The divider values both sets at $\frac12$, so the divider is content with whichever set remains and does not envy the chooser. The chooser picks the set she values at least as much as the other, so she does not envy the divider. Hence the division is envy-free. ∎

prompt:
*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

A division $d_1$ *dominates* $d_2$ if at least one player gets strictly greater total value in $d_1$ and no player gets less. A division is *Pareto efficient* if no division dominates it. *Divide and Choose* (two players): one player (the divider) splits $G$ into two sets, each worth exactly $\frac12$ to the divider; the other player chooses the set she prefers (by her own values) and the divider gets the remaining set.

Prove, or disprove by finding a counterexample, that Divide and Choose always results in a Pareto efficient division.
answer: False. With $v_1=(1,0)$ and $v_2=(0,1)$ on $(C,V)$, the divider can cut each good in half and both players get only $\frac12$.

solutions.title: Counterexample
solutions.body:
Let $G=\{C,V\}$ with
$$\begin{array}{c|cc} & v_1 & v_2 \\ \hline C & 1 & 0 \\ V & 0 & 1\end{array}$$Player 1 may divide $G$ into two bundles each consisting of half of $C$ and half of $V$; each is worth $\frac12$ to Player 1. Player 2 also values each at $\frac12$ and takes either one. Both players receive $\frac12$. But giving $C$ to Player 1 and $V$ to Player 2 gives each of them value $1$, which dominates. So the outcome of Divide and Choose need not be Pareto efficient.

prompt:
*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

A division is *envy-free* if for all players $i\ne j$, $v_i(G_i)\ge v_i(G_j)$, where $G_k$ is what player $k$ receives.

Consider the following attempt to generalize Divide and Choose to three players: Player 1 first divides $G$ into three sets, each worth exactly $\frac13$ to Player 1. Then Player 2 chooses the set she prefers, Player 3 chooses the set he prefers from the remaining two, and Player 1 gets the last set. Is this procedure envy-free? Prove, or disprove by finding a counterexample.
answer: No: Player 3 may envy Player 2, who chose first.

solutions.title: Counterexample
solutions.body: Let $G=\{A,B,C\}$ with $v_1=(\frac13,\frac13,\frac13)$, $v_2=(0.5,0.25,0.25)$ and $v_3=(0.8,0.1,0.1)$ on $(A,B,C)$. Player 1 may divide $G$ into the three sets $\{A\},\{B\},\{C\}$ (each worth $\frac13$ to him). Player 2 chooses $\{A\}$ (her favorite). Player 3 must choose between $\{B\}$ and $\{C\}$ and gets only $0.1$, but values Player 2's set $\{A\}$ at $0.8$. So Player 3 envies Player 2 and the procedure is not envy-free.

prompt:
*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

A division is *envy-free* if for all players $i\ne j$, $v_i(G_i)\ge v_i(G_j)$, where $G_k$ is what player $k$ receives.

The cake $g$ is the interval $[0,1]$ and each player has a continuous nonnegative density function (total integral $1$) giving the value of any piece. *Two-player Moving Knife Procedure:* a knife is swept from position $0$ to the right; as soon as either player believes the portion to the left of the knife is worth $\frac12$ of the whole, they call stop and the cake is cut there. The player who called stop receives the left piece and the other player receives the right piece.

Prove that this procedure results in an envy-free division.
answer: The stopper values both pieces at $\frac12$. The other player had not yet reached $\frac12$ on the left, so by continuity she values the right piece at least $\frac12$.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body: Each player's value of the left piece is a continuous nondecreasing function of the knife position, going from $0$ to $1$, so some player reaches $\frac12$ and the procedure stops (the first time any player does). Suppose Player $A$ stops it at position $x$. Then $A$ values the left piece at exactly $\frac12$ and so the right piece at exactly $\frac12$; $A$ is content with the left piece. The other player $B$ did not call stop earlier, so at all positions before $x$ and, by continuity, at $x$ itself $B$ values the left piece at most $\frac12$. Hence $B$ values the right piece at least $\frac12$, at least as much as the left piece, and $B$ does not envy $A$. (If both reach $\frac12$ simultaneously, both are indifferent.) ∎

prompt:
*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

A division is *proportional* if each of the $n$ players receives total value at least $\frac1n$ by their own value function.

The cake $g$ is $[0,1]$ and each player has a continuous nonnegative density. *Moving Knife Procedure for $n$ players:* a knife is swept from the left; as soon as any of the $n$ players believes that the portion of the (current) cake to the left of the knife is worth $\frac1n$ of the whole (current) cake to them, they call stop. The cake is cut there and the player who called stop receives the piece to the left of the knife. The procedure is then repeated on the remainder of the cake with the remaining $n-1$ players (each now measuring against the value of the remainder).

Prove that this procedure results in a proportional division: every player receives at least $\frac1n$ of the value they place on the whole cake.
answer: Induct on $n$: the stopper gets exactly $\frac1n$; every other player values the remainder at least $\frac{n-1}n$ and by induction gets at least $\frac1{n-1}$ of that, i.e. at least $\frac1n$.

solutions.title: Induction on n
solutions.body:
We prove: for any $n$ players and any (sub)cake, each player ends up with at least $\frac1n$ of the value she assigns to that cake. For $n=1$ the single player takes everything.

Assume it holds for $n-1$ players. In the first round some player stops the knife at the first moment any player reaches $\frac1n$ of her value of the whole; she receives exactly $\frac1n$ of her value. Every other player $j$ has not yet reached $\frac1n$, so (by continuity, at the stopping point) values the left piece at most $\frac1n$ of the whole; hence she values the remainder at least $1-\frac1n=\frac{n-1}n$ of the whole. By the induction hypothesis applied to the remainder with $n-1$ players, she finally receives at least $\frac1{n-1}$ of her value of the remainder, which is at least $\frac1{n-1}\cdot\frac{n-1}n=\frac1n$ of her value of the whole. So all $n$ players get at least $\frac1n$. ∎

prompt:
*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

The cake $g$ is $[0,1]$ and each player has a continuous density that is positive on $(0,1)$ (total integral $1$), giving the value of any piece. Consider this two-player *Moving Knife* variant: Player 1 holds two knives. The first starts at the left edge of the cake and the second at the position $m$ where Player 1 believes the cake is split into two halves of equal value. Player 1 sweeps both knives slowly to the right so that the piece between the knives always has value exactly $\frac12$ to Player 1, until the right knife reaches the right edge. As soon as Player 2 agrees that the piece between the knives is worth $\frac12$ to her, she says stop; the cake is cut at the knives, the center piece goes to Player 2 and the rest goes to Player 1.

(i) Prove that the procedure always terminates.
(ii) Prove that the resulting division is *exact*: both players believe that each of the two players received total value exactly $\frac12$ (so it is also envy-free and proportional).
answer: (i) Player 2's value of the center piece is continuous and takes values $g_0$ and $1-g_0$ at the start and end, so by the intermediate value theorem it equals $\frac12$ at some moment. (ii) At that moment both players value the center piece at exactly $\frac12$, hence the rest also at $\frac12$.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
(i) Let $g(t)$ be Player 2's value of the center piece at time $t$; it is continuous since the knives move continuously. At the start the center piece is $[0,m]$, with $g(0)=g_0$. The sweep ends with the right knife at $1$ and the center piece $[a^*,1]$, where Player 1 values $[a^*,1]$ at $\frac12$; since Player 1's density is positive, $a^*=m$, so the final center piece is $[m,1]$, with Player 2's value $1-g_0$. If $g_0=\frac12$ she stops immediately. Otherwise $g_0-\frac12$ and $(1-g_0)-\frac12$ have opposite signs, so by the intermediate value theorem there is a time $t'$ with $g(t')=\frac12$, and Player 2 stops the procedure then. (Player 2 is not required to stop earlier, so the procedure stops at the first such $t'$.)

(ii) When the procedure stops, the center piece is worth exactly $\frac12$ to Player 1 (by the construction) and exactly $\frac12$ to Player 2 (by her stopping condition). The rest of the cake is therefore also worth $1-\frac12=\frac12$ to each of them. So each player values both pieces at exactly $\frac12$: the division is exact. In particular nobody values the other's piece more than their own (envy-free) and everyone gets at least $\frac12$ (proportional). ∎

prompt:
*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

*Divide and Choose* (two players): one player (the divider) splits $G$ into two sets, each worth exactly $\frac12$ to the divider; the other player chooses the set she prefers (by her own values) and the divider gets the remaining set.

Here $A,B,C$ are divisible, homogeneous goods with true value functions
$$\begin{array}{c|cc} & v_1 & v_2 \\ \hline A & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ B & 0.3 & 0.4 \\ C & 0.5 & 0.3\end{array}$$Suppose Players 1 and 2 divide $G$ using Divide and Choose with Player 1 as the divider, and Player 1 knows Player 2's value function. By carefully selecting the initial division (knowing Player 2 will then choose whichever set is worth more to her), Player 1 can guarantee himself a total value (by his true values) of $\frac{x}{1000}$ for many integers $x$. Compute the largest such integer $x$.

solutions.title: Maximize against Player 2's choice
solutions.body:
Player 1 wants to end with a bundle $S$ that Player 2 does not choose, i.e. worth strictly less than $\frac12$ to Player 2 (so the other bundle is strictly better for her), while maximizing the value of $S$ to Player 1. This is a fractional knapsack: value to Player 1 per unit of Player 2's value is $\frac{0.5}{0.3}$ for $C$, $\frac{0.3}{0.4}$ for $B$, and $\frac{0.2}{0.3}$ for $A$. So Player 1 should take all of $C$ (cost $0.3$ in Player 2's value) and then as much of $B$ as possible: a fraction $\beta$ of $B$ costs $0.4\beta$, and the budget is just under $0.2$, so $\beta<\frac12$. For any $\epsilon>0$ he can split $G$ into $\{C,(\frac12-\epsilon)B\}$ and $\{A,(\frac12+\epsilon)B\}$: Player 2 values these at $0.5-0.4\epsilon$ and $0.5+0.4\epsilon$ and takes the second, leaving Player 1 the first, worth $0.5+0.3(\frac12-\epsilon)=0.65-0.3\epsilon$ to him.

The supremum $0.65$ is not attained, so the largest value $\frac{x}{1000}$ he can guarantee has $x=649$ (any $\epsilon\le\frac1{300}$ gives at least $0.649$, and $0.65-0.3\epsilon<0.65$ always, so $0.650$ cannot be guaranteed).

**Answer: 649**

prompt:
*Setup.* There are $n$ players and a finite set $G$ of goods to divide among them. Each player $i$ has a value function $v_i$: values are nonnegative, additive, $v_i(\varnothing)=0$ and $v_i(G)=1$. Goods may be indivisible (given whole to one player) or divisible and homogeneous (a fraction $x$ of a good is worth $x$ times its value). A player's total value in a division is the sum of the values (to that player) of what they receive.

Suppose a third party chooses the division that maximizes the total value received by the players *according to the value functions they report*. With
$$\begin{array}{c|cc} & v_1 & v_2 \\ \hline A & 0.2 & 0.3 \\ B & 0.3 & 0.4 \\ C & 0.5 & 0.3\end{array}$$(for divisible goods $A,B,C$) the maximal division with honest reports is $\{1:(C),\ 2:(A,B)\}$, which yields a total value of $0.5$ to Player 1. If Player 1 lies about his value function to the third party but Player 2 tells the truth, what is the maximal true total value (using his original value function) that Player 1 could achieve?

solutions.title: Lie to win B and C
solutions.body:
The third party gives each good to the player who reports the higher value (ties may be split). Player 2 reports truthfully: $A=0.3$, $B=0.4$, $C=0.3$. Player 1's report must also sum to $1$, so he can win a set of goods only if his reports on them exceed Player 2's: to win $B$ and $C$ he reports more than $0.4$ and more than $0.3$ for them (e.g. $B=0.405$, $C=0.305$, $A=0.29$), which is possible since $0.405+0.305<1$. Winning all three goods would require reports exceeding $0.3+0.4+0.3=1$, which is impossible, and winning $A$ and $B$ or $A$ and $C$ is worth less to him. Winning $B$ and $C$ gives him true value $0.3+0.5=0.8$, the best possible.

**Answer: 0.8**
